label: explain2-track-6
one_line: We test whether a computer-checked rulebook can say if a claimed flying fish glide breaks the laws of physics.
what: We are building a referee for animal claims. A claim might be "a fish glided 50 metres". The referee checks the claim against rules of physics. A proof program has checked those rules step by step. The referee gives one of three answers: ruled out, not ruled out, or cannot tell. It never says "proved". Our test case is the flying fish, because researchers measured fish bodies in a wind tunnel. The newest glide test is only a plan with bets written down first. It has no result yet.
why: Claims about animals are often repeated from paper to paper. Nobody redoes the sums. This project is for catching that. When we reopened the sources, almost every number held. But one headline pair of numbers came from two different simulated flights. A referee that checks the sums is useful. It should also say plainly what it cannot judge. It could be used on many other animals later. For example, a long glide seen at sea may include paddling on the water. Our simple rule does not cover that, so the referee says "cannot tell".

steps.text: Measure the fish. Researchers put stuffed fish models in a wind tunnel. Air blew past them at 12 metres per second, about 43 kilometres per hour. They recorded how much lift and drag the body makes. Lift is the upward push of air. Drag is the backward pull of air.
steps.picture: Holding a paper plane out of a car window and feeling it pull up and back.

steps.text: Work out the slowest speed that keeps the fish up. We used a model fish of 0.06 kilograms, about the weight of a large egg. We combined its weight with the best lift number from the tunnel. The answer is 9.85 metres per second. That is about the speed of a fast cyclist. Below it, the fish drops. This is called the stall speed.
steps.picture: A bicycle that wobbles and falls once you go too slowly.

steps.text: Work out a distance limit. A fish that launches fast can trade its speed for distance, like a cyclist coasting off a hill. The best lift-to-drag ratio found was 4.37. That means the air gives 4.37 units of lift for every 1 unit of drag. The rule is: distance = 4.37 x (launch speed squared minus stall speed squared) / (2 x 9.81). The number 9.81 is how fast gravity speeds things up.
steps.picture: Coasting downhill: the faster you start, the farther you roll.

steps.text: Try the rule on real numbers. Launch at 10 metres per second. Speed squared is 100. Stall speed squared is about 97.1. The gap is 2.9. Then 4.37 x 2.9 / 19.62 gives 0.646 metres. That is about the length of your arm. So a 10 metres per second launch buys less than one metre of glide at the same height. To glide 50 metres, half a football pitch, the same rule needs a launch of about 17 metres per second. That is about 61 kilometres per hour, a car in town.
steps.picture: Rolling a toy car off a very low ramp: it stops within an arm's length.

steps.text: Write the rule as a proof. A proof program, this one called Lean, checks every step of the logic. It checks that the distance limit really follows from the numbers we typed in. It does not check that the numbers are right. Those come from measurements and papers.
steps.picture: A strict teacher who marks each line of a sum, but does not know if you copied the starting numbers correctly.

steps.text: Write down bets before looking. For example, a launch at 10 metres per second should buy under 1 metre of glide at the same height. Each bet says which result would count against us.
steps.picture: Writing your guess in a sealed envelope before the race.

steps.text: Re-check the sources. We downloaded the original papers and data. We redid the sums with a short program anyone can rerun.
steps.picture: Checking a restaurant bill line by line.

steps.text: Look for rival explanations. Long flights might have another cause. One example is the fish beating its tail on the water surface, which gives it extra push.
steps.picture: A long jumper who seems to leap far, but took a running start you did not count.

steps.text: Report the answer in three ways only. The referee says ruled out, not ruled out, or cannot tell. "Not ruled out" never means "possible" or "true".
steps.picture: A court that can say guilty, not guilty, or not enough evidence, but never "innocent for sure".

wrong_if: We bet that the stall speed and the distance limit hold for a fish that glides with no tail paddling. We would be wrong if a careful, measured glide with no extra push went clearly farther than the limit allows. We would also be wrong if a fish like our model could fly slower than 9.85 metres per second. We have a second bet. A live fish leaping from an aquarium at 3.9 to 5.2 metres per second, about a brisk jog, should not glide far at the same height. If a measured long glide came from such a launch, that bet would fail.
could_go_wrong: Every wind tunnel number comes from stuffed fish models. A live fish may behave differently.
The distance rule only works if the fish is neither climbing nor sinking. A fish pushed upward, for example by rising air, could go farther than the rule says.
Field distances such as 50 metres were reported by others. They were not measured by us. We found no public raw record of real glide tracks.
The simulation paper gives a 45.4 metre distance and a 13.2 metre height. These came from different runs, so it is easy to misread them as one flight.
The aquarium paper gives take-off speeds but not how long each leap lasted. So one planned test cannot be done with it.
Paddling on the water may explain long flights. The simple rule cannot judge those.
Some of our own bets would have come true whatever the data showed. Passing them tells us little. They add less than they seem to.
The proof program checks the logic only. The numbers fed into it can still be wrong or out of date.

questions.a: We reopened the original papers and reran the sums with short programs. Almost all numbers matched. Anyone can rerun them using the commands listed below.
We did not rerun the proof program ourselves for the newest proof. We found no public raw glide-track data. We did not read every figure in the simulation paper.
No. It is a plan with bets written first. We found no results for it yet.
It is for checking animal claims against physics, and saying plainly when a check is not possible. The flying fish is only the first test case.

questions.q: What does the proof program prove?
questions.a: It proves that the rule's steps follow from each other. For example, it proves that a given stall speed and lift-to-drag ratio lead to a given distance limit. It does not prove that the measured numbers are right.

questions.q: How does 4.37 become a distance limit?
questions.a: Take launch speed squared minus stall speed squared. Multiply by 4.37. Divide by twice the pull of gravity, which is 19.62. For a 10 metres per second launch this gives 0.646 metres.

questions.q: Does "not ruled out" mean the claim is true?
questions.a: No. It only means our rules could not knock the claim down.

questions.q: Why would a fish glide farther than the rule allows?
questions.a: It may paddle its tail on the water first, which adds push. The rule leaves that out. So a longer distance seen at sea does not mean a law of physics is wrong.

questions.q: How slowly can the model fish fly?
questions.a: About 9.85 metres per second, about the speed of a fast cyclist. That uses a 0.06 kilogram fish and the best lift number measured in the tunnel.

questions.q: How fast do live fish leap in an aquarium?
questions.a: They were estimated at 3.9 to 5.2 metres per second, about a brisk jog. That is well below the 9.85 floor. But it is a different fish from the model.

questions.q: Why does a simulation headline need care?
questions.a: Its 45.4 metre glide and 13.2 metre height came from two different runs. All the runs began at 20 metres per second, about 72 kilometres per hour.

glossary.plain: Software that checks each step of a maths argument and refuses it if any step is missing. It checks the logic, not the measurements.
A tube where fast air blows over a model so we can measure the forces on it.
The upward push that air gives a moving wing or body.
The backward pull of air that slows something moving.
Lift divided by drag. A ratio of 4.37 means 4.37 units of lift for each unit of drag. A higher number means a farther glide.
The slowest speed at which the body still gets enough lift to stay up. Below it, the fish drops.
Moving through the air without flapping or any push.
A glide that stays at about the same height instead of sinking.
A computer model that imitates what would happen in real life.
Skimming along the water surface with the tail beating, which gives extra push.
Pushed upward, for example by rising air.
Reported by others in an older paper, not measured by the people now quoting it.
A result we write down before looking, so we can later see if we were wrong.
A measure of speed. 10 metres per second is about 36 kilometres per hour, the pace of a fast cyclist.
A jump out of the water made by a live fish in a tank.
Our name for the checker that tests claims against rules.
A label our check program prints when a number we recomputed does not match the paper's number.

left_out: Claim that tail-paddling on the water is the 'strongest rival': only partly supported, since no source says 'strongest'. It is shown here as one rival, not the strongest.
Claim that only two open datasets exist for gliding animals: we could not fully verify this broad negative. We say only that we found no public raw glide tracks for fish.
Claim that the newest proof passed the proof program with no errors: the checker did not rerun it, so it is not stated as fact.
Claim that version 1.8.1 of our own rule list fixed the wrong flagging of gliding fish: the fix was made in version 1.7.0, so no credit is given to 1.8.1.
Exact counts for the fin-size data (49 fish, 14 large): only partly reproduced, so they are not used.
Several of our own bets were reported as unable to fail on their own. This is mostly the author's reading, so it is only mentioned as a general risk.
